stages.name: Government intervention: permits and failure
stages.title: Government intervention: permits and failure
stages.sub: After this, the student can weigh the drawbacks of tradeable permits and judge whether government intervention is actually worth it.

steps.q: A regulator issues pollution permits and lets firms trade them, creating a market price for pollution. If the regulator sets the total number of permits too high, will the pollution cut be as big as hoped?
steps.right: No, too little pollution would be cut
steps.wrong: Yes, the market price fixes this automatically
steps.hint: The number of permits decides how much pollution is allowed in total.

steps.q: Every firm's emissions have to be measured and checked, and every permit trade has to be tracked and enforced. Is that free to run?
steps.right: No, it costs money and staff to run
steps.wrong: Yes, the market runs itself once set up
steps.hint: Someone has to check what firms actually emit and verify every trade.

steps.q: A factory now has to buy permits to keep polluting at home, but a country next door has no such scheme. What might the factory's owner consider doing?
steps.right: Moving production to the country with no scheme
steps.wrong: Paying for extra permits and staying put
steps.hint: If polluting is cheaper abroad, where might the firm choose to produce instead?

steps.q: A wrong permit cap distorts the price of pollution, monitoring adds cost, and firms may relocate abroad. If you looked at a minimum wage, a subsidy, or a tax instead, could each of these run into its own version of a mis-set price, extra cost, or an unintended side effect?
steps.right: Yes, the same kinds of problems show up
steps.wrong: No, only permits run into these problems
steps.hint: Distorted signals, admin costs and unintended consequences are not unique to one policy tool.
steps.pre: So these causes of failure show up

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: A policy fixes a market failure but its own costs and side effects turn out to be larger than the problem it solved. Should the government still intervene?
steps.right: No, only if the benefits outweigh the costs
steps.wrong: Yes, any fix for a market failure is worth doing
steps.hint: Intervening is not automatically good just because there was a market failure to begin with.
